A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Syntax-Knowledge framework and retain corresponding theoretical and experimental sections. Text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G are readable and support a complete comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-biography experiments on scaling, frequency-dependent knowledge acquisition, and SFT-versus-CPT forgetting in Section 5 and Appendix F.

after.justification: v5 retains those original experiments and adds Fineweb-edu training results and PopQA evaluations in Section 5.4 and Figure 6.

M1.justification: The parametric syntax encoder, Pitman–Yor knowledge mixture, hierarchical generation procedure, and perplexity objective remain substantively unchanged. Revisions concern mathematical assumptions and explanations rather than a new algorithm or architecture.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates controlled synthetic biographies and associated questions. v5 adds natural-language training and scaling evaluation on Fineweb-edu and factual question answering on PopQA, substantially extending the represented data and evaluation domain.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparisons retain uniform versus power-law sampling and SFT versus CPT. The new real-world experiments compare model sizes without introducing another competing method; additional related-work citations are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The new PopQA evaluation measures accuracy across model sizes using object popularity, o_pop, as a frequency proxy. Fineweb-edu adds data- and model-scaling evaluations. The retained synthetic experiments keep their splits, training budgets, and configurations; changed Figure 5 fits do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Figure 6(c) adds a real-world check of whether capacity-dependent failure on rare knowledge persists on PopQA. The existing property-heterogeneity and SFT/CPT capacity analyses are retained in Figures 8–9 and Table 2.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed or repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The added scaling fits and accuracy curves retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Figure 5(a) replaces the synthetic model-scaling fits: decay exponents for sampling powers 1.20, 1.35, and 1.50 change from 0.37/0.48/0.57 to 0.26/0.38/0.48, with changed offsets. Figure 6 adds Fineweb-edu scaling and PopQA knowledge-cutoff results. These are revised or newly reported results, not demonstrated same-setting performance improvements. Table 2 is unchanged.

T1.justification: Assumption 5.1 replaces pointwise log-likelihood Lipschitzness with a quadratic KL-divergence bound, accompanied by revised covering arguments in Appendix G.4. v5 also revises the Fisher-information expansion, conditional-independence derivation, and fine-tuning approximation and rate. These materially alter the mathematical justification despite retaining the principal scaling rates.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain the compression perspective, Syntax-Knowledge model, scaling-law explanations, and frequency-dependent knowledge acquisition and hallucination claims. The shorter fine-tuning contribution summary still refers to conclusions retained in Appendix E; real-world experiments add support rather than redefine the central contribution.

C2.justification: v5 explicitly states that uniform sampling lies outside its Pitman–Yor theory and distinguishes test redundancy from averaged cumulative Bayesian redundancy in Appendix D.1. Section 5.4 adds interpretations of natural-language irreducible loss and explains differing fitted offsets through finite data and model sizes. The original forgetting and knowledge-acquisition mechanisms remain.

D1.justification: Section 5.4 provides limited technical information for the new experiments, specifying reuse of the synthetic-experiment architecture and the popularity proxy. Appendix F's generation recipe, tokenizer, hyperparameters, model configurations, and code reference remain unchanged. Detailed real-world splits and training procedures are not supplied.

R1.justification: Section 6 substantially expands positioning against distribution-based scaling theories, adding Hutter, Michaud and colleagues, Brill, and Maloney and colleagues, followed by explicit distinctions concerning compression, syntax, and redundancy analysis. Additional knowledge-memory and hallucination literature further broadens the positioning.

P1.justification: The overall narrative and appendix organization remain recognizable. v5 adds background explanation of scaling laws, refines terminology and examples, reorganizes some appendix explanations, and updates authorship and acknowledgments. Most existing prose is retained rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v5 adds multipanel Figures 6 and 7 for real-world results and three-dimensional structure-function illustrations. It revises the Figure 3 schematic and several existing plots' axes, legends, and styling, and relocates Table 3 beside Appendix F. Original appendix Figures 6–7 become Figures 8–9 without changing their underlying images.

improvement.justification: The real-world checks extend empirical support beyond v1's synthetic setting, while clearer assumptions and mathematical corrections improve parts of the exposition. Gains are limited by sparse real-world protocol details and unexplained Figure 5 refits. There is also a new indexing error in Appendix D.2: Phi_-2 includes phi1, yet the displayed mutual-information expansion separately adds its contribution again.
